checks.claim: Key: particles in ice vibrate in place, packed close together
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'particles are tightly packed and vibrate in fixed positions'; Grokipedia Solid: 'atoms or molecules oscillating around equilibrium sites in a lattice'; Wikipedia State of matter: 'cannot move freely but can only vibrate'. Ice is less dense than liquid water (sciencelearn.org.nz), but that comes from its open lattice; neighbouring molecules are still in close contact, so 'packed close together' stands at grade level.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Resting quite still, packed close together'
checks.note: NASA eClips names 'molecules in a solid are not moving' as a misconception; Grokipedia Solid: solids exhibit vibrational motion. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Sliding past one another, close together' (that is a liquid)
checks.note: Sliding past one another is the liquid picture ('remain close together but can move past one another'); solid particles are 'held in fixed positions'. Wrong for ice.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Flying about, far apart from one another' (that is a gas)
checks.note: Gas particles are 'widely separated from one another and move freely'; not ice.

checks.claim: Context: solid particles packed tightly, held in fixed places, so ice keeps its shape; never still, each vibrates on its own spot even in a freezer
checks.note: Grokipedia Solid: 'This arrangement gives solids a definite shape and volume'; vibration about lattice sites. A freezer (about -18 C) is far above absolute zero, so the molecules certainly vibrate.

checks.claim: Key: a liquid's particles stay close but slide past one another, so it takes a new shape
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'particles that are close together but can slide past one another'; 'a fixed volume but the ability to conform to the shape of its container'. Grokipedia Liquid: 'closely packed but possess sufficient kinetic energy to move relative to one another'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'They stay in fixed places but bend to fit'
checks.note: Fixed places is the solid picture; particles do not bend (a documented misconception of particles taking macroscopic properties, RSC). Wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'They move far apart and fly about freely'
checks.note: That is a gas; liquid particles stay closely packed and the liquid keeps its volume. Wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'They sit still until the pouring pushes them'
checks.note: Grokipedia Liquid: molecules form clusters that 'continually rearrange'; liquid particles are always moving. Wrong.

checks.claim: Context: close together so the water keeps its volume; not held in fixed places; slide past one another all the time, so the water flows into its container's shape
checks.note: 'maintain a fixed volume while adopting the shape of its container'; continual rearrangement. Measuring cylinder to dish: same volume, new shape, true.

checks.claim: Key: a gas fills its container because its particles move fast and freely in all directions
checks.note: Grokipedia Gas: particles 'widely separated from one another and move freely at high speeds'; gases 'spontaneously expand to fill available space when unconstrained'. Grokipedia Kinetic theory: motion 'chaotic and isotropic (equal in all directions)'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Its particles push one another away from a distance'
checks.note: Real gases: 'Attractive interactions pull molecules toward each other'; 'Repulsive forces ... dominate at very short ranges' (contact only). Ideal model: no forces except during collisions. So no push from a distance; repulsion as the cause of spreading is a documented student misconception (RSC, about 20% of 16+ year-olds). Wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Its particles are drawn toward the glass walls of the jar'
checks.note: Particles reach the walls by their own motion and collisions ('elastic collisions with each other and the container walls'); no pull toward the walls spreads the gas. A trace of gas can cling to a surface (adsorption), but that is not why a gas fills a jar. Wrong as a reason.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Its particles swell up until they fill the jar'
checks.note: Particles expanding is a documented misconception; Grokipedia Kinetic theory treats molecules' volume as negligible compared with the container. Wrong.

checks.claim: Context: gas particles move fast in straight lines in every direction until they hit another particle or a wall
checks.note: 'Between collisions, molecules travel in straight lines at constant speeds'; collisions with each other and the walls.

checks.claim: Context: nothing holds them together; they do not push one another away from a distance or get drawn to the walls; they meet only when they collide
checks.note: This is the ideal-gas model ('no attractive or repulsive forces between the particles except during instantaneous collisions'). Real gases have a weak attraction between particles and a slight cling to surfaces, far too weak to hold the gas together or to explain its spreading, so the statement is a fair grade-level simplification. Optional polish: 'Nothing holds them together, and no push or pull spreads them: their own motion does.'

checks.claim: Stem: air pumped out, a little gas let in, soon fills the whole jar
checks.note: A gas let into an evacuated space expands at once to fill it (free expansion). 'All the air' is the usual idealisation.

checks.claim: Stem number: the tank holds about 11 litres of water (internal volume)
checks.note: Grokipedia: the AL80 'has an actual internal volume of about 11 liters'; Wikipedia: 'approximately 11 litres'; Luxfer spec: 11.1 L water volume.

checks.claim: Stem number: a pump squeezes about 2,300 litres of air into it
checks.note: Wikipedia: nominal 'free gas' capacity of 80 cubic feet (2,300 L) at 3,000 psi (210 bar); 80 cu ft = 2,265 L. The true capacity is a little less: about 77.4 cu ft, about 2,190 L, at 3,000 psi / 207 bar (Luxfer spec sheet, https://static1.squarespace.com/static/55031996e4b0562b390e52e4/t/5dd593f1f20d1d4b14f41999/1574278157284/Luxfer-Cylinder-Spec-Sheet.pdf, via dive-shop listings). 'About 2,300' is the documented nominal figure and within 5% of the true one, so it stands; 'about 2,200' would match the true fill a shade better if the writer wants it exact.

checks.claim: Key: air's particles are far apart and can be pushed closer
checks.note: 'far apart from one another compared to their size'; 'Most of the volume of a gas ... is composed of the empty space between the particles'; 'gases are easily compressed'. Grokipedia Gas: 'high compressibility due to the large average distance between particles'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Air's particles shrink smaller as they are squeezed in'
checks.note: Particles contracting is a documented misconception; compression shrinks the space between particles, not the particles. Wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Air's particles join up into fewer, bigger particles'
checks.note: The nitrogen and oxygen molecules stay the same molecules at 200 bar; compressed air is the same mixture, just denser. Wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Air's particles stop moving and stack up tidily in rows'
checks.note: Air's critical temperature is about -140 C, so at room temperature no pressure can liquefy it, let alone freeze it into an ordered solid; its particles keep moving. Wrong.

checks.claim: Context: most of a gas is empty space; pressing pushes particles closer, here into about a two-hundredth of the room the air took before
checks.note: 11 L / 2,265 L nominal = 1/206; 11.1 L / 2,190 L true = 1/197; the fill pressure is about 207-210 bar. 'About a two-hundredth' is right.

checks.claim: Context: the air in the tank is still a gas, its particles still on the move
checks.note: Above its critical temperature (air about 133 K) a gas cannot be liquefied by pressure alone; a filled scuba tank holds compressed gas, not liquid air (Engineering Toolbox / Linde glossary agree).

checks.claim: Context: water can hardly be squeezed because its particles are already in close contact
checks.note: Grokipedia Liquid: 'nearly incompressible under normal conditions'; Grokipedia State of matter ties near-incompressibility to particles already in close contact.

checks.claim: Key: as the ring melts, the gold's particles break free of their fixed places
checks.note: 'As a solid is heated, its particles vibrate more rapidly'; 'the disruptive vibrations of the particles of the solid overcome the attractive forces'; 'the organization of the particles within the solid structure begins to break down'. Grokipedia State of matter: 'increased thermal energy disrupts the lattice, allowing particles greater mobility'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'They melt and turn soft, as the ring does'
checks.note: Particles melting is a documented misconception ('the particles melted or died'); a gold atom does not melt. Wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'They slow down and sink into a heap'
checks.note: Heating makes the particles vibrate more rapidly, not slow down. Wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'They break into smaller bits of gold'
checks.note: Particles 'break up' is a documented misconception; a gold atom is the smallest bit of gold and stays whole when it melts. Wrong.

checks.claim: Stem: the ring glows, then slumps into a shining pool of liquid gold
checks.note: Solids begin to glow dull red near 525 C (Draper point); gold melts at about 1,064 C (Grokipedia Melting gives 1,337 K), so it glows long before it melts. Ring alloys melt a little lower (18 ct about 920-980 C), still well above the glow.

checks.claim: Context: heat gives the particles more energy; at the melting point they break free; a particle does not melt, soften or break, only the way the particles are held together changes
checks.note: Grokipedia Melting: heat input is needed 'to overcome the intermolecular forces holding the solid together'; 'thermal energy causes atoms to oscillate with amplitudes large enough to disrupt positional order'.

checks.claim: Key: the ink spreads sooner because hot water's particles move faster and bump the ink about
checks.note: What is wrong: in an unstirred beaker the visible spreading comes mostly from CONVECTION currents, not from particles bumping the ink (diffusion). The Goethe-Institut activity for this exact demo: 'sometimes explained as showing how heat affects DIFFUSION, but it is really a demonstration of CONVECTION' (hot water loses heat at its top and sides, the cooled water sinks and sets the bottle circulating). Dou, Hogan, Kossover, Spuck and Young, 'Defusing Diffusion', American Biology Teacher 75(6), 2013 (https://discovery.fiu.edu/display/pub176474), tested such demos in microgravity and found most of the dispersion comes from convection; Stony Brook's lab-demo page says 'residual currents in the water account for much of this "diffusion"'. Numbers: Grokipedia Diffusion gives about 1e-9 m2/s for diffusion in liquids, which spreads ink only about 0.35 mm in a minute and takes about 14 hours to cross 1 cm; Grokipedia also notes convection makes 'it appear as if diffusion is faster than it truly is'. What is true: hot water's particles do move faster (and diffusion does speed up with heat), but that is the smaller part of why the drop spreads 'much sooner'. The key is still the only defensible choice (every wrong choice is wrong), but its 'why' is the classroom misconception the stem invites. Fix (best): ask about the particles, not the cause of the spreading, e.g. 'What is different about the particles of the hot water?' with key 'They are moving faster' and the same kinds of wrong choices (bigger, pulling harder, melted); context: heat gives the particles more energy so they move faster; the faster particles jostle the ink, and as the hot water cools at its top and sides it also sets slow currents stirring, which do most of the carrying. Fix (minimal): keep the stem, key 'Hot water's particles move faster, so the ink is stirred and jostled more', and give the context the currents.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Hot water's particles are smaller, leaving the ink more room'
checks.note: Particles do not change size with temperature (RSC lists particles expanding/contracting as misconceptions). Wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Hot water's particles pull harder on the drop of ink'
checks.note: Heating raises the particles' kinetic energy; it does not strengthen their pull. Wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Hot water's particles melt the ink into much finer bits'
checks.note: Ink is already a liquid; particles melting or breaking up is a documented misconception. Wrong.

checks.claim: Context: hot water's particles move faster; they knock the ink's particles about harder and more often, and the ink spreads sooner; the moving water particles carry it along
checks.note: Each sentence is true in itself, but together they teach molecular bumping as THE reason, which the demo literature above calls refuted: the currents do most of the carrying. Add the currents, e.g. 'The faster particles jostle the ink, and as the hot water cools at its top and sides it sets slow currents moving, which carry the ink round the beaker. Both come from the heat.'

checks.claim: Stem: unstirred hot and cold beakers, one drop each; the hot one spreads much sooner
checks.note: University of Iowa demo: 'the drop in the hot water diffuses much faster than the drop in the cold water'. The observation is right; only the explanation is the problem.

checks.claim: Key: the size of each particle is the same in the vapour as in the ice
checks.note: Sciencelearn: 'Even though the water's physical form changes, its molecules stay the same'; UWEC: 'the composition of the molecules ... remains the same'; Grokipedia Thermal expansion and RSC: heating raises the separation between particles, and particles swelling is a documented misconception. The particle model treats the particle's size as unchanged, and that is the true lesson here. Nuance for the lead, not a fault: the water molecule's O-H bond is about 0.958 angstrom in the vapour and about 0.97-1.01 angstrom in ice and liquid water (stretched a few percent by the hydrogen bonds; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3801132/ and arXiv 2502.15557), so the molecule is, if anything, a hair LARGER in the ice. That is a few-percent effect against the misconception's large swelling (steam takes about 1,700 times the room), so 'the same size' is a fair grade-6 simplification. If an airtight key is wanted: 'Each particle is still the same water particle'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The speed of the particles'
checks.note: 'adding heat increases the kinetic energy (motion) of the molecules'; vapour just boiled off at about 100 C moves much faster than ice from a freezer. Different, so wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The space between the particles'
checks.note: Water becoming steam takes up about 1,700 times the room; gas particles are 'far apart'. Different, so wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The pull between the particles'
checks.note: In ice the hydrogen bonds are 'numerous enough and strong enough to prevent the water molecules from flowing past one another'; in vapour 'all of the interactions are broken and the water molecules are free to wander off'. The pull actually acting is very different. (The force law between two molecules at a given distance is the same in every state, but the stem asks what is the same about the particles in the vapour and in the ice, and the pull they feel is not.) Wrong.

checks.claim: Context: the very same particles; none grows or shrinks; boiling gives particles enough energy to escape the liquid and fly off as a gas; what changes is how they move and how they are held together
checks.note: Boiling: the average kinetic energy rises until molecules throughout the liquid have enough to vaporize (writer's source; consistent with UWEC). 'None grows or shrinks' carries the same few-percent bond-length nuance noted on the key; acceptable at grade level.

checks.claim: Key: the vapour's particles slowed down and came close together at the cool glass
checks.note: Grokipedia: condensation allows 'molecules to lose kinetic energy and come together to form a denser liquid state'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'They sped up and stuck fast to the glass'
checks.note: Cooling lowers the particles' average kinetic energy; they slow, not speed up. 'Water in the air sticks to the glass' is a recorded child explanation (RSC); the drops do cling to the glass, but 'sped up' makes the choice wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'They shrank smaller and packed into drops'
checks.note: Particles contracting is a documented misconception. Wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'They joined into bigger, heavier particles'
checks.note: RSC records the misconception of 'molecules breaking up on boiling and reforming on condensing'; the water molecules stay whole H2O molecules, they only gather into a drop. Wrong.

checks.claim: Stem: after a hot shower the mirror is covered in drops that formed from water vapour in the warm, damp air
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'Condensation forms when the window surface temperature drops below the dew point temperature of the indoor air'; 'water vapor into liquid droplets on a cold glass surface'.

checks.claim: Context: the cool glass takes energy from the vapour; particles slow until they cling together, close-packed as in a liquid; this is condensation, the reverse of evaporation
checks.note: 'This process is the reverse of evaporation or vaporization'; the heat released on condensing passes into the cooler glass.

unit_notes: 1 error, 7 ok. The error is the hot/cold ink drop (031fd0536d): the visible spreading in an unstirred beaker is mostly convection currents, not particles bumping the ink (Goethe-Institut activity; Dou et al. 2013, American Biology Teacher; diffusion in liquids is about 1e-9 m2/s, under half a millimetre a minute). Best fix: ask what is different about the hot water's particles (key: moving faster) and let the context name the currents. Advisory only, no change needed: the 2,300 L tank figure is the nominal 80 cu ft (true fill about 2,190 L); 'particles keep their size' is the standard model, while the real O-H bond is a few percent longer in ice than in vapour; 'not drawn to the walls' in the gas context is the ideal-gas model.
